learn.hook: When your class votes on whether the picnic should be at the zoo or at a lakeside park, you are using an idea that people have been arguing about for about 2,500 years!
points: The word democracy comes from two Greek words: 'demos' (the people) and 'kratos' (rule or power). So democracy means rule by the people.
Athens, a city-state in ancient Greece, is the best-known early democracy (around the 5th century BCE). Its citizens met in an Assembly and voted directly on laws, war and peace.
Athenian democracy was limited: only adult male citizens could take part. Women, enslaved people and foreigners living in Athens were left out.

In a direct democracy, citizens decide matters themselves. In a representative democracy, citizens elect representatives who make decisions on their behalf. Big modern countries such as India are representative democracies.
Abraham Lincoln, President of the USA, described democracy in 1863 as 'government of the people, by the people, for the people'.

example.q: Think it through: Citizens of Athens could gather in one place and vote on every law. Why can't all voters of India do the same today?
steps: Athens was a single city, and the number of citizens who could take part was fairly small.
India is a huge country with crores of voters spread over villages, towns and cities.
It is impossible for all of them to meet together and debate every law, every day.
So Indians elect representatives (MPs, MLAs, councillors, panchayat members) who discuss and decide for them and answer to them at the next election.
example.answer: Because of India's huge size and population, direct democracy for every decision is not practical, so India uses representative democracy.

learn.reallife: A school student council, a housing society committee and a gram sabha meeting in a village are all small examples of people taking part in decisions, either directly or through people they choose.

games.title: Match the word to its meaning
pairs: Famous early democracy in ancient Greece
Citizens elect people to decide for them

games.title: Direct or representative?
items: Athenian citizens voting in their Assembly on going to war
All adult villagers in a gram sabha discussing the village plan together
A whole class voting by a show of hands on the picnic spot
All members of a small housing society voting at a meeting on building a park
Voters electing an MP to the Lok Sabha
A class electing a monitor to speak for it at school meetings
MLAs making laws in a state Vidhan Sabha
Residents electing a municipal councillor for their ward

quiz.q: The Greek word 'demos', from which 'democracy' comes, means:
quiz.explain: 'Demos' means the people and 'kratos' means rule or power. Together they give 'rule by the people'.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up 'demos' (people) with 'kratos' (power)

quiz.q: Which ancient city-state is best known as an early democracy where citizens voted directly on laws?
quiz.explain: In Athens, around the 5th century BCE, citizens met in an Assembly and voted directly on important matters.
quiz.mistake: Remembers 'ancient' but not which city practised direct democracy

quiz.q: Who could take part in the Assembly of ancient Athens?
quiz.explain: Only adult male citizens could vote in Athens. Women, enslaved people and foreign residents were excluded, so it was a limited democracy.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the first democracy included everyone, as modern democracies do

quiz.q: In which form of democracy do citizens elect people to make laws on their behalf?
quiz.explain: In a representative democracy, voters choose representatives such as MPs and MLAs who make laws for them.
quiz.mistake: Confuses representative democracy with direct democracy, where citizens decide everything themselves

quiz.q: Why do large countries like India use representative democracy rather than direct democracy?
options: Crores of citizens cannot all meet and decide every matter together
Citizens are not allowed to vote in large countries
Direct democracy was banned by the United Nations
Representatives are chosen by the king
quiz.explain: With crores of voters spread across a vast country, it is not practical for everyone to debate and vote on every law, so people elect representatives.
quiz.mistake: Thinks representative democracy means citizens have no say at all

quiz.q: Who described democracy as 'government of the people, by the people, for the people'?
quiz.explain: US President Abraham Lincoln used these words in his Gettysburg Address in 1863.
quiz.mistake: Links a famous democratic quote with another well-known leader

quiz.q: All 40 families of a housing society meet and vote together on whether to build a children's park. This is an example of:
quiz.explain: Every member votes on the decision personally, without choosing representatives, so it is direct democracy.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any vote is representative democracy, even when people decide for themselves

quiz.q: Roughly how long ago did democracy flourish in ancient Athens?
quiz.explain: Athenian democracy flourished around the 5th century BCE, which is roughly 2,500 years ago.
quiz.mistake: Confuses ancient Athens with modern democracies such as the USA, which began about 250 years ago

teach.ask: Gappu flaps in: 'What does democracy mean? And what is the difference between direct democracy and representative democracy?'
teach.praise: Wow, I get it! The people rule, either by deciding themselves or by electing representatives. Even my nest can vote now!
teach.nudge: But who actually makes the decisions in each type? Do the people decide themselves, or do they choose someone?

learn.hook: Long before ballot boxes, a village in Tamil Nadu chose its leaders by pulling palm-leaf slips out of a pot. India's democratic story is very old!
points: The Rigveda mentions assemblies called the sabha and the samiti, where members of the community met to discuss common matters.

Around the 6th century BCE, some states in north India were ganas or sanghas, governed by an assembly of many people instead of a single king. The Vajji (Vrijji) confederacy, with its capital at Vaishali in present-day Bihar, is a well-known example.
The Buddhist sangha took decisions in meetings of monks, following rules for discussion and voting.

Inscriptions at Uttaramerur in Tamil Nadu, from the Chola period (10th century CE), describe how members of the village assembly were chosen: names were written on palm leaves, put in a pot and drawn out. This was called kudavolai.

Modern India's Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950 and gave universal adult franchise: every adult citizen got the right to vote, whatever their religion, caste, gender, wealth or education.

example.q: Think it through: Why are the Uttaramerur inscriptions important for understanding democracy in India?
steps: They are written records carved in stone, so they give solid evidence and not just stories.
They describe rules for choosing members of a village assembly and the qualifications needed.
This shows that ideas such as choosing members by a fixed, written procedure existed in India over a thousand years ago.
Such traditions are part of the background to India's modern democracy.
example.answer: They are clear evidence that Indian villages had rule-based ways of choosing assembly members over 1,000 years ago.

learn.reallife: Gram sabhas and panchayats in Indian villages today continue the old tradition of local communities discussing and deciding their own matters.

games.title: India's democratic journey
items: Rigveda mentions the sabha and samiti
Vajji gana-sangha governs from Vaishali
Uttaramerur inscriptions describe village assembly elections
Constitution of India comes into force
First general elections of independent India
Voting age lowered from 21 to 18

items.text: The Rigveda mentions two assemblies, the sabha and the ___.
Vaishali was the capital of the ___ confederacy.
The Uttaramerur inscriptions belong to the ___ period.
Drawing palm-leaf slips with names from a pot was called ___.

quiz.q: Which ancient text mentions the assemblies called sabha and samiti?
quiz.explain: The sabha and samiti are Vedic assemblies mentioned in the Rigveda.
quiz.mistake: Picks a famous historical book without matching it to the Vedic period

quiz.q: What was special about a gana or sangha in ancient India?
options: It was governed by an assembly of many people, not by one hereditary king
It had no rules of any kind
It was ruled by a foreign emperor
quiz.explain: In ganas or sanghas, decisions were taken by an assembly of members rather than a single king.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every ancient Indian state was a monarchy

quiz.q: Vaishali, capital of the Vajji confederacy, is in which present-day state?
quiz.explain: Vaishali is in present-day Bihar, in the middle Ganga plains where several ganas existed.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the ancient ganas with the Ganga plains of north India

quiz.q: Uttaramerur, famous for inscriptions about village assembly elections, is in:
quiz.explain: Uttaramerur is in Tamil Nadu. Its Chola-period inscriptions describe how village assembly members were chosen.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the Chola period with south India

quiz.q: How did the kudavolai system at Uttaramerur work?
options: Names written on palm leaves were put in a pot and drawn out
The king picked his favourite person
The richest person automatically became the member
People voted by pressing a button on a machine
quiz.explain: Names of eligible people were written on palm leaves, placed in a pot (kudam) and drawn out, so the choice followed a fixed procedure.
quiz.mistake: Imagines old methods as either royal choice or modern machines

quiz.q: Universal adult franchise in India means:
options: Every adult citizen has the right to vote, without discrimination
quiz.explain: From 1950, every adult citizen got the vote, irrespective of religion, caste, gender, wealth or education.
quiz.mistake: Thinks voting rights in India depend on education, gender or wealth, as in some older systems

quiz.q: What is the minimum age to vote in India today?
quiz.explain: The 61st Constitutional Amendment (1988) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18 years.
quiz.mistake: Remembers the old voting age of 21 or confuses it with the age to contest elections (25 for the Lok Sabha)

quiz.q: When were the first general elections of independent India held?
quiz.explain: The first general elections were held between October 1951 and February 1952, after the Constitution came into force in 1950.
quiz.mistake: Assumes elections were held in the year of independence

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: 'Did India have any democratic ideas before 1950? Tell me some examples!'
teach.praise: Amazing! From Vedic assemblies to palm-leaf pots to every adult voting in 1950. India's democracy has deep roots!
teach.nudge: Can you name an ancient assembly, a gana, or the village with the palm-leaf voting pot?

learn.hook: If one person decided everything in your school, from the timetable to the canteen menu, and nobody could complain, would you be happy? Democracy is about having a say.
points: In a democracy, rulers are chosen by the people in free and fair elections held regularly, and voters have a real choice. Every adult has one vote and each vote has equal value.
Rule of law: the law applies equally to everyone, including those in power. Fundamental rights of citizens are protected by the Constitution and the courts.
Separation of powers divides work among the legislature (makes laws), the executive (carries them out) and the judiciary (interprets laws and settles disputes), so that no one holds all power.
Accountability and transparency: the government must answer to the people and work openly. The Right to Information Act, 2005 lets citizens ask for government information.

Democracy is valued because it makes governments answerable, allows peaceful change, respects dignity and equality, and lets mistakes be corrected. Its challenges include slow decisions, misuse of money and misinformation, and protecting the rights of weaker groups.
A free media and grassroots democracy (panchayats and municipalities, given constitutional status by the 73rd and 74th Amendments in 1992) keep citizens informed and involved.

example.q: Think it through: Country X holds an election every five years, but the ruling party jails all opposition candidates before voting day. Is Country X a democracy?
steps: Holding an election is necessary for democracy, but it is not enough.
The election must be free and fair, and people must have a real choice between candidates.
If opposition candidates are jailed, voters cannot really choose and the rulers cannot be voted out.
So the rulers are not truly accountable to the people.
example.answer: No. Without a free and fair election and real choice, Country X is not a democracy even though it holds elections.

learn.reallife: When a news report exposes a broken road, citizens file an RTI application, or a gram sabha questions how village funds were spent, democracy is working at the everyday level.

games.title: Democratic or not?
items: Citizens elect leaders in regular, free elections
Courts can rule against the government
Newspapers can criticise ministers
Every adult's vote has equal value
A ruler stays in power for life and cannot be voted out
All opposition parties are banned
Only people who own land may vote
Laws do not apply to the ruler's family

games.title: True or false?
items: In a representative democracy, laws are made by representatives elected by the people.
Laws are made by representatives who are chosen by, and answer to, the people.
Holding an election, by itself, is enough to make a country democratic.
Elections must also be free and fair and give voters a real choice.
Rule of law means the law applies equally to ordinary citizens and to people in government.
Nobody is above the law in a democracy.
The judiciary is the organ of government that makes laws.
The legislature makes laws; the judiciary interprets them and settles disputes.
The 73rd Amendment of 1992 gave constitutional status to panchayats.
It made panchayats a constitutional part of grassroots democracy. The 74th Amendment did the same for municipalities.
In a democracy, citizens are not allowed to criticise the government.
Freedom of expression lets citizens and the media question and criticise the government.

quiz.q: The principle 'one person, one vote, one value' means:
options: Only one person in a village may vote
quiz.explain: Every adult citizen has one vote, and every vote carries the same weight.
quiz.mistake: Thinks some people's votes can count for more than others'

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of accountability in a democracy?
options: Ministers answering questions asked by members in Parliament
A ruler refusing to explain his decisions
Results of an election being kept secret
quiz.explain: Accountability means those in power must explain and answer for their actions, for example during Question Hour in Parliament.
quiz.mistake: Confuses accountability with simply having power

quiz.q: A minister's car jumps a red light and the minister is fined just like any other driver. This shows:
quiz.explain: Rule of law means the same law applies to everyone, including people in power.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up rule of law with other democratic features

quiz.q: Which organ of government interprets laws and settles disputes?
quiz.explain: The judiciary (the courts) interprets laws and settles disputes. The legislature makes laws and the executive carries them out.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the roles of the three organs of government

quiz.q: Which is the strongest reason why democracy is considered better than other forms of government?
options: The government is answerable to the people and can be changed peacefully
Decisions are always taken very quickly
quiz.explain: Democracy does not guarantee perfect leaders, but it makes governments answerable and lets people change them through elections.
quiz.mistake: Believes democracy means perfect or speedy government

quiz.q: Which is a common criticism of democracy?
options: Courts are not allowed to exist
Decisions can take longer because of debate and consultation
quiz.explain: Because many people are consulted and debate takes time, decisions in a democracy can be slow.
quiz.mistake: Lists features of non-democracies as criticisms of democracy

quiz.q: How does a free media help democracy?
options: It informs citizens and can expose wrongdoing by those in power
It makes laws for the country
quiz.explain: A free press keeps people informed and holds the powerful to account by reporting on their actions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the media has the powers of the government or courts

quiz.q: In which year was the Right to Information Act passed, letting citizens ask for government information?
quiz.explain: The Right to Information Act was passed in 2005 to promote transparency in government.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the year with other milestones such as 1950 (Constitution) or 1992 (73rd and 74th Amendments)

teach.ask: Gappu is curious: 'What makes a country a real democracy, and why do people prefer it?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! Fair elections, equal rights, the rule of law and answerable leaders. No wonder people prefer democracy!
teach.nudge: You've told me about elections. But what about rights, the rule of law, or leaders answering to the people?

learn.hook: India's general election is one of the biggest events organised anywhere on Earth: polling teams carry machines by road, boat and on foot so that even remote voters can vote!
points: India is divided into areas called constituencies. The Lok Sabha has 543 constituencies, and each elects one Member of Parliament (MP). Each state is also divided into assembly constituencies that elect MLAs. Elections are normally held every 5 years.
Every citizen aged 18 or above whose name is on the electoral roll (voter list) can vote. Voting is secret, and an indelible ink mark on the finger helps prevent anyone voting twice.

The Election Commission of India (ECI), set up on 25 January 1950 under Article 324 of the Constitution, is an independent body that conducts elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President.

Main steps: dates are announced and the Model Code of Conduct begins, candidates file nominations, nominations are checked, campaigning takes place, people vote on polling day, and votes are counted and results declared.
Votes are cast on Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs). A VVPAT machine prints a slip showing the chosen symbol so the voter can check it. NOTA ('None of the Above') lets a voter reject all candidates.
Some constituencies are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes: only candidates from these groups can contest there, but all voters of the constituency vote.

example.q: Think it through: Why is voting in India kept secret?
steps: If others could see how someone voted, powerful people could threaten or bribe voters.
Secrecy lets every voter choose freely, without fear of their boss, neighbours or even family.
This protects the freedom and fairness of the election.
example.answer: Secret voting protects voters from pressure and fear, so that every vote is a free choice.

learn.reallife: National Voters' Day is celebrated on 25 January, the day the Election Commission was set up. Ask an adult at home to show you the voter ID card (EPIC) and the ink mark after voting.

games.title: Steps of an election
games.prompt: Arrange the steps of an election from first to last
items: Election dates announced and Model Code of Conduct begins
Candidates file nomination papers
Nomination papers are checked (scrutiny)
Parties and candidates campaign
Voters cast their votes on polling day
Votes are counted and results declared

items.q: Normal term of the Lok Sabha (years)?
Year the Election Commission was set up?
First Chief Election Commissioner of India?

quiz.q: Which body conducts elections to the Lok Sabha?
quiz.explain: The Election Commission of India conducts elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President. State Election Commissions conduct panchayat and municipal elections.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the Election Commission of India with State Election Commissions or the courts

quiz.q: What does a VVPAT machine do?
options: Counts the population of a constituency
Prints a slip showing the symbol the voter chose, so the voter can check it
quiz.explain: VVPAT (Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail) shows a printed slip of the chosen symbol for a few seconds so the voter can verify the vote.
quiz.mistake: Thinks VVPAT is the voting or counting machine itself

quiz.q: What is the Model Code of Conduct?
options: A law that sets the voting age
Guidelines that parties, candidates and governments must follow during elections
A list of all voters in a constituency
A rule for how to design an EVM
quiz.explain: It is a set of guidelines from the Election Commission. For example, the government should not announce new schemes to win votes once elections are announced.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the Model Code of Conduct with the electoral roll or election laws

quiz.q: What does pressing NOTA on an EVM mean?
options: The voter supports the ruling party
The voter wants the election cancelled immediately
The voter rejects all the candidates
quiz.explain: NOTA stands for 'None of the Above'. It lets a voter record that they do not support any candidate. It was added in 2013 after a Supreme Court judgment.
quiz.mistake: Thinks NOTA cancels the election or counts for some party

quiz.q: In a constituency reserved for Scheduled Castes, who can vote?
options: All registered voters of that constituency
quiz.explain: Reservation decides who can contest, not who can vote. Only Scheduled Caste candidates can stand, but every registered voter there votes.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a reserved seat also limits who can vote

quiz.q: What is an electoral roll?
options: The list of people eligible to vote in a constituency
quiz.explain: The electoral roll, or voter list, contains the names of all eligible voters. It is updated regularly.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the voter list with a list of candidates or results

quiz.q: Why is indelible ink put on a voter's finger?
options: To stop the same person from voting twice
To show which party the person voted for
quiz.explain: The ink mark cannot be removed easily for many days, so polling staff can see that the person has already voted.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the ink reveals the voter's choice, which would break secrecy

quiz.q: The Election Commission of India was set up on 25 January of which year?
quiz.explain: It was set up on 25 January 1950, a day before the Constitution came into force. National Voters' Day is celebrated on this date.
quiz.mistake: Links the Election Commission with Independence Day (1947) or the first elections (1951–52)

teach.ask: Gappu waves a tiny flag: 'Who runs elections in India, and what happens from the announcement to the result?'
teach.praise: Super! The Election Commission runs it, adults of 18+ on the voter list vote secretly on EVMs, and then the votes are counted. Hooray for elections!
teach.nudge: Who organises the election? And what are the steps between announcement and the results?

learn.hook: In a race, the runner who crosses the line first wins, even if just by a step. India's Lok Sabha elections work in a similar way!
points: First-Past-The-Post (FPTP): the country is divided into constituencies, each electing one representative. The candidate with the most votes wins, even with less than half of all votes.
Under FPTP, a party's share of seats can be very different from its share of votes, because only the winner in each constituency gets the seat.

Proportional Representation (PR): a party gets seats in proportion to its share of votes. In list PR, used in countries such as Israel and the Netherlands, votes are counted for parties, and each party's seats are filled from its list of candidates.

India uses FPTP for Lok Sabha and state Vidhan Sabha elections. It uses PR by single transferable vote (voters rank candidates by preference) to elect Rajya Sabha members (by MLAs), the President and the Vice-President.
India chose FPTP for direct elections because it is simple for voters, gives every area its own representative, and usually produces clear results and stable governments.

example.q: Think it through: In a constituency, Asha gets 42,000 votes, Bilal 38,000 and Charan 20,000 (total 1,00,000). Who wins under FPTP, and did the winner get a majority?
steps: Under FPTP, the candidate with the highest number of votes wins.
Asha has the most votes (42,000), so Asha wins the seat.
42% is less than half, so 58% of voters chose someone else, yet Asha still wins.
example.answer: Asha wins with 42% of the votes, which is the most votes but not a majority.

learn.reallife: When results are shown on TV, the Lok Sabha seat count of a party is often very different from its percentage of votes. That is FPTP at work.

quiz.q: In a constituency, Asha gets 42,000 votes, Bilal 38,000 and Charan 20,000. Who wins under FPTP?
options: Nobody, because no one got more than half
quiz.explain: Under FPTP the candidate with the most votes wins. A majority (more than half) is not needed.
quiz.mistake: Thinks FPTP requires the winner to get more than 50% of votes

items: Asha
Bilal
Charan

quiz.q: In the same contest (42,000 + 38,000 + 20,000 votes), what percentage of the votes did the winner get?
quiz.explain: 42,000 out of 1,00,000 votes is 42%. So the winner won with less than half of the votes.
quiz.mistake: Adds the losers' votes (58%) or assumes the winner must have 50%

items: Asha
Bilal
Charan

quiz.q: A legislature has 200 seats and uses pure proportional representation. A party wins 25% of the votes. About how many seats should it get?
quiz.explain: Under PR, seats follow vote share: 25% of 200 = 50 seats.
quiz.mistake: Takes the percentage itself as the number of seats
steps: = 50 seats

quiz.q: Which elections in India are held using the First-Past-The-Post system?
quiz.explain: Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha elections use FPTP. The President, Vice-President and Rajya Sabha members are elected by proportional representation through the single transferable vote.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all Indian elections use the same system

quiz.q: How is the President of India elected?
options: By an electoral college through proportional representation by single transferable vote
Directly by all voters through FPTP
quiz.explain: Elected MPs and elected MLAs form the electoral college, and they vote using the single transferable vote, a form of PR.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the President is chosen directly by the people like an MP

quiz.q: What is a major drawback of the FPTP system?
options: It is too complicated for voters to understand
A party's share of seats can be much larger or smaller than its share of votes
It needs the whole country to be one constituency
quiz.explain: In FPTP only the winner in each constituency gets the seat, so votes for losing candidates do not turn into seats.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the features of FPTP with those of list PR

quiz.q: Why did India choose FPTP for Lok Sabha elections?
options: It guarantees that every party gets seats equal to its votes
It is simple for voters and gives each area its own representative
It was required by the British Parliament
It removes the need for an Election Commission
quiz.explain: FPTP is easy to understand, links each constituency with one accountable representative, and tends to give clear results.
quiz.mistake: Thinks FPTP gives perfectly proportional results, which is a feature of PR

quiz.q: Which country uses proportional representation with the whole country treated as one constituency?
quiz.explain: In Israel, seats in its parliament are shared out among parties according to their national vote share. India, the UK and Canada use FPTP for their national parliament elections.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that the UK and Canada, like India, use FPTP

teach.ask: Gappu scratches his head: 'What is the difference between FPTP and proportional representation? Which one does India use?'
teach.praise: Now I see! In FPTP the top vote-getter wins; in PR seats follow vote share. India uses FPTP for the Lok Sabha and PR for the Rajya Sabha and President!
teach.nudge: You explained one system. What about the other, and where does India use each one?

learn.hook: For about 21 months, from 1975 to 1977, many rights that Indians took for granted were suspended. Then voters had their say at the ballot box. This chapter of our history shows why democratic safeguards matter.
points: The Constitution allows a national emergency under Article 352 when the country faces a grave threat. During an emergency, the central government gets extra powers and some fundamental rights can be suspended.

Background: on 12 June 1975, the Allahabad High Court declared Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's 1971 election from Rae Bareli void. At the same time, a large opposition movement led by Jayaprakash Narayan was demanding her resignation.

On 25 June 1975, President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed proclaimed a national emergency on the grounds of 'internal disturbance', on the advice of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. The government said this was needed to maintain order and stability.

During the Emergency, many fundamental rights were suspended, newspapers were censored, many opposition leaders and others were detained without trial, and elections were postponed. The 42nd Amendment (1976) made many changes to the Constitution.

Lok Sabha elections were held in March 1977. The ruling Congress lost, and the Emergency was withdrawn on 21 March 1977. The Janata Party formed the government, and Morarji Desai became the first non-Congress Prime Minister.

The 44th Amendment (1978) added safeguards: 'internal disturbance' was replaced by 'armed rebellion', the President can declare an emergency only on the written advice of the Cabinet, and the rights in Articles 20 and 21 (including life and personal liberty) cannot be suspended.

example.q: Think it through: What lessons did India's democracy learn from the Emergency?
steps: It showed that the emergency powers in the Constitution could be used to suspend rights for a long time.
It showed how important a free press, independent courts and the right to protest are in a democracy.
In 1977, voters used their vote to change the government peacefully.
Parliament then passed the 44th Amendment so that emergency powers would be harder to misuse.
example.answer: Rights need strong safeguards, citizens and institutions must stay alert, and elections let people change governments peacefully.

learn.reallife: Whenever people discuss press freedom, the independence of courts or limits on government power, the experience of 1975–77 is often remembered.

games.title: Emergency timeline
games.prompt: Arrange the events from earliest to latest
items: Allahabad High Court verdict on the Rae Bareli election (June 1975)
Emergency proclaimed (25 June 1975)
42nd Amendment passed (1976)
Lok Sabha elections held (March 1977)
Morarji Desai becomes Prime Minister (March 1977)
44th Amendment adds safeguards (1978)

games.title: True or false?
items: The Emergency of 1975 was proclaimed on the grounds of 'internal disturbance'.
That was the ground given in 1975. The 44th Amendment later replaced it with 'armed rebellion'.
During the Emergency, newspapers faced censorship.
Newspapers had to get some news approved by censors before printing it.
The 1975 Emergency lasted for about five years.
It lasted about 21 months, from June 1975 to March 1977.
In the 1977 Lok Sabha elections, the party in power at the Centre lost.
The Janata Party won, and Morarji Desai became Prime Minister.
Today, a national emergency can be declared only on the grounds of war, external aggression or armed rebellion.
After the 44th Amendment (1978), these are the only grounds under Article 352.
The right to life and personal liberty (Article 21) can still be suspended during an emergency.
The 44th Amendment made sure Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even during an emergency.

quiz.q: On which date was the national emergency proclaimed in 1975?
quiz.explain: The Emergency was proclaimed on 25 June 1975. On 12 June 1975 the Allahabad High Court had given its verdict on the Rae Bareli election.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the High Court verdict date with the date the Emergency was proclaimed

quiz.q: Who was the President of India who proclaimed the Emergency in 1975?
quiz.explain: President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed proclaimed the Emergency on the advice of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.
quiz.mistake: Remembers a President from a nearby period but not the one in office in 1975

quiz.q: Under which Article number of the Constitution can a national emergency be proclaimed?
quiz.explain: Article 352 deals with a national emergency. Article 356 is about President's Rule in a state and Article 360 about financial emergency.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the national emergency with President's Rule (Article 356) or financial emergency (Article 360)

quiz.q: Which of these happened during the Emergency of 1975–77?
options: The first general elections were held
Newspapers were censored and many opposition leaders were detained
quiz.explain: Press censorship and detention of opposition leaders without trial were major features of the Emergency.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up events from different periods of Indian history

quiz.q: Who led the large opposition movement in 1974–75 that demanded the Prime Minister's resignation?
quiz.explain: Jayaprakash Narayan (JP) led the movement. Ambedkar, Patel and Rajendra Prasad had passed away before the 1970s.
quiz.mistake: Picks a famous national leader without checking the time period

quiz.q: What was the result of the Lok Sabha elections of March 1977?
options: The Janata Party formed the government and Morarji Desai became Prime Minister
The ruling party won every seat
The President dissolved all political parties
quiz.explain: Voters defeated the ruling Congress. The Janata Party formed the first non-Congress government at the Centre, led by Morarji Desai.
quiz.mistake: Does not realise the 1977 elections changed the government

quiz.q: What change did the 44th Amendment (1978) make to emergency provisions?
options: It allowed emergencies to be declared without any reason
'Internal disturbance' was replaced by 'armed rebellion' as a ground
It made the President directly elected
quiz.explain: The 44th Amendment narrowed the grounds to war, external aggression or armed rebellion, and added other safeguards.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the amendment increased emergency powers rather than limiting them

quiz.q: About how long did the Emergency of 1975–77 last?
quiz.explain: It lasted from 25 June 1975 to March 1977, which is about 21 months.
quiz.mistake: Does not work out the period from June 1975 to March 1977

teach.ask: Gappu looks worried: 'What was the Emergency, and what did India change afterwards so it would not happen the same way again?'
teach.praise: Thank you! In 1975 rights were suspended and the press censored, voters changed the government in 1977, and the 44th Amendment added safeguards. Lesson learnt!
teach.nudge: When did it happen, and what happened to people's rights? How did it end, and what safeguards came later?

topics.title: What governance means and who governs

learn.hook: Clean water from the tap, a streetlight that works, a school bus that runs on time: each one is a small sign of governance quietly doing its job!
points: Government means the institutions that hold the authority to make and enforce decisions for the country: the legislature makes laws, the executive puts them into action, and the judiciary interprets laws and settles disputes. India has governments at the Union, state and local levels.

Governance means the whole process of making decisions, carrying them out and checking whether they worked, for the welfare of the public. Simply put, government is the institution; governance is how the work actually gets done.

Many people take part in governance: elected representatives, ministries and departments, civil servants, courts, panchayats and municipalities, and also citizens, the media, civil society groups, researchers and businesses.

Principles of good governance include participation, transparency (decisions and information are open), accountability (those in authority answer for their actions), the rule of law (the same laws apply equally to all), responsiveness, inclusiveness and effectiveness.

Indian traditions have long discussed just rule. Rajadharma is the duty of a ruler to protect the people and work for their welfare, and Mahatma Gandhi used 'Ram Rajya' to describe an ideal of fair rule where even the weakest person gets justice. India's national motto 'Satyameva Jayate' ('Truth alone triumphs') comes from the Mundaka Upanishad. The Sengol, a ceremonial sceptre that stands for just rule in the Tamil tradition, was installed in the new Parliament building in 2023.

example.q: Think it through: After a night of very heavy rain, roads in a town are flooded. Is this a job for just one office?
steps: The municipal body must clear the drains and pump out water.
Traffic police must divert vehicles, and the electricity department must make fallen wires safe.
The health department must prevent water-borne diseases, and disaster response teams may need to rescue people.
All of them must share information and work together, and residents must be told what to do.
example.answer: No. Handling the flood needs many departments to coordinate and communicate. That coordinated process of deciding, acting and checking is governance.

learn.reallife: In Delhi, the Delhi Jal Board is a government body; how it plans the water supply, tests water quality and fixes complaints is governance. The same is true of your town's municipal body collecting waste every morning.

games.title: Institution or process?
items: Parliament
The Supreme Court
A municipal corporation
A State Legislative Assembly
Planning how to clear flooded roads
Checking whether garbage is collected every day
Consulting residents before building a park
Putting a department's spending details online

games.title: Principles of good governance
pairs: Information about decisions is open to the people
Those in authority must answer for their actions
The same laws apply equally to everyone
People take part in decisions that affect them
No group is left out of public services
Acting on people's needs within a reasonable time

quiz.q: Which statement best describes governance?
options: The process of making, carrying out and checking decisions for public welfare
Only the act of voting in an election
The political party that won the last election
quiz.explain: Governance is the whole process of deciding, acting and monitoring for the public good. It is ongoing, not a single building, event or party.
quiz.mistake: Confuses governance with a place, an election or a party

quiz.q: Which organ of government mainly puts laws and policies into action?
quiz.explain: The executive (ministers, ministries, departments and civil servants) implements laws and policies. The legislature makes laws and the judiciary interprets them.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the roles of the three organs of government

quiz.q: A city department puts its full budget and spending details on its website for anyone to read. Which principle of good governance does this show most clearly?
quiz.explain: Making information about decisions and spending open to the public is transparency.
quiz.mistake: Does not link open information with transparency

quiz.q: In the state assembly, members question a minister about why a scheme failed, and the minister must explain. Which principle is at work?
quiz.explain: Accountability means those in authority must answer for their decisions and actions. Questions in the legislature are one way of holding the executive accountable.
quiz.mistake: Does not see answering for actions as accountability

quiz.q: What does 'Rajadharma' mean?
options: A kind of election in ancient India
The duty of a ruler to protect the people and work for their welfare
The name of an ancient law court
quiz.explain: Rajadharma is the idea that a ruler's power comes with duties: protecting the people and working for their well-being.
quiz.mistake: Guesses from the word 'raja' without knowing the idea of a ruler's duty

quiz.q: India's national motto 'Satyameva Jayate' is taken from which text?
quiz.explain: 'Satyameva Jayate', meaning 'Truth alone triumphs', comes from the Mundaka Upanishad. It is written below the Lion Capital in the State Emblem of India.
quiz.mistake: Picks a famous text without knowing the source of the motto

quiz.q: Who takes part in governance?
options: Government institutions along with citizens, the media, civil society and others
Only judges of the Supreme Court
quiz.explain: Governance involves government institutions at every level, and also citizens, the media, civil society groups, researchers and businesses.
quiz.mistake: Thinks governance is done by one person or by the government alone

quiz.q: A town builds ramps, Braille signs and accessible toilets at its bus stand so that persons with disabilities can use it easily. Which principle does this show?
quiz.explain: Inclusiveness means public services are designed so that no group, including persons with disabilities, is left out.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect access for everyone with inclusiveness

teach.ask: Gappu flutters down: 'Government and governance sound the same to me! What is the difference, and what makes governance good?'
teach.praise: Now I get it! Government is the institution, governance is how decisions are made, carried out and checked, and good governance is open, answerable and fair to all. Tweet-tastic!
teach.nudge: You told me one part. Is governance a building or a process? And which principles make it good?

learn.hook: Why does your school bus stop exactly where it does, and why is there a zebra crossing outside your school? Someone had to notice a problem, think of options and decide!
points: A public policy is a planned course of action taken by the government to solve a public problem or meet a public need. It is 'public' because it uses public resources and affects society. A company's work-from-home rule is a policy, but not a public policy.

A policy sets the broad goals and direction. Programmes and schemes are specific plans that put a policy into action. For example, Khelo Bharat Niti 2025 is India's national sports policy, and it involves several ministries, such as Youth Affairs and Sports, and Education.

Policies usually move through a cycle: identify the problem or need, set priorities, consult stakeholders and draft options (formulation), get formal approval (adoption), put it into action (implementation), monitor and evaluate, and use feedback to revise the policy.

Stakeholders are people and groups affected by or involved in a policy, such as citizens, elected representatives, departments, local bodies, experts, civil society, the media and businesses. Consulting them makes a policy more practical and fair.

Money, staff and time are limited, so governments must set priorities and check feasibility: Is it affordable? Is it technically possible? Who will carry it out? Evidence and data help decide what comes first.

example.q: Think it through: Every morning there is a traffic jam at your school gate. How could a policy be made to fix it?
steps: Identify the problem: collect facts, such as how many vehicles arrive between 7:30 and 8:00.
Consult stakeholders: parents, students, teachers, bus drivers, traffic police and nearby shopkeepers.
Draft options: a separate drop-off zone, different arrival times for different classes, more school buses, a walking group for nearby students.
Check feasibility (cost, space, safety), choose the best option, and get the principal and school committee to approve it.
Try it out, check whether the jam reduces, and change the plan if needed.
example.answer: Follow the policy cycle: identify, consult, draft options, choose and adopt, implement, then check and improve.

learn.reallife: The Swachh Bharat Mission, launched on 2 October 2014, aimed to make India clean and free from open defecation. It needed the Union government, states, municipalities, panchayats and ordinary citizens to work together.

games.title: The policy cycle
games.prompt: Arrange the stages of making a public policy from first to last
items: Identify the problem and set priorities
Consult stakeholders and draft options
Adopt the policy through formal approval
Implement the policy
Monitor and evaluate the results
Use feedback to revise the policy

games.title: Public policy or not?
items: A national policy on vaccinating children
Municipal rules for separating wet and dry waste
India's national sports policy, Khelo Bharat Niti
A state policy to bring safe drinking water to villages
A company's work-from-home rule for its staff
A coaching centre's rule on mobile phones in class
A housing society's timings for its swimming pool
A cricket club's rule on practice timings

quiz.q: What is a public policy?
options: A rule a family makes for its own children
A planned course of action by the government to solve a public problem or meet a public need
A promise printed in an advertisement
Any decision taken by a private company
quiz.explain: A public policy is made by the government, uses public resources and affects society as a whole.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any rule made by any group is a public policy

quiz.q: Which of these is a public policy?
options: A shop's policy on returning goods
A family rule on screen time
A national policy on vaccinating children
A company's rule on annual leave
quiz.explain: A national vaccination policy is made by the government for the whole society. The others are rules of private groups or families.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up an organisation's own policy with a public policy

quiz.q: Which stage usually comes FIRST when a public policy is made?
quiz.explain: A policy begins by identifying a problem or need. Only then can options be drafted, adopted and implemented.
quiz.mistake: Starts with action before understanding the problem

quiz.q: What happens during the formulation stage of a policy?
options: Stakeholders are consulted, options are drafted and their cost and feasibility are checked
Courts punish people who break the policy
quiz.explain: Formulation means preparing the policy: consulting, drafting options and checking whether they are affordable and practical.
quiz.mistake: Confuses formulation with later stages or with elections

quiz.q: Why should a government consult stakeholders before finalising a policy?
options: To make the policy take as long as possible
Because every citizen must sign every policy
Because people who are affected know the problem first-hand, which makes the policy more practical and fair
quiz.explain: People affected by a problem often understand it best. Their views help avoid mistakes and make the policy work in real life.
quiz.mistake: Thinks consultation is only a delay or a legal formality

quiz.q: How is a policy different from a programme or scheme?
options: A policy sets broad goals and direction; a programme is a specific plan to achieve them
A programme sets the broad direction; a policy is one small task
They are exactly the same thing
A policy is made only by courts
quiz.explain: The policy gives the big picture and goals. Programmes and schemes are the detailed plans that turn those goals into action.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the meanings of policy and programme

quiz.q: Why do governments have to set priorities among public needs?
options: Because some citizens do not matter
Because money, staff and time are limited, so the most urgent needs must be met first
Because policies are chosen by lottery
Because only one policy is allowed each year
quiz.explain: Resources are limited, so governments use evidence to decide which needs are most urgent, such as safe drinking water.
quiz.mistake: Thinks priorities mean ignoring people rather than managing limited resources

quiz.q: What does 'adoption' of a policy mean?
options: The policy is formally approved by the proper authority, such as the Cabinet, a legislature or a municipal council
The policy is copied from another country
The policy is shown on television
quiz.explain: Adoption is the formal approval of a policy by the authority that has the power to decide, after which it can be implemented.
quiz.mistake: Takes 'adoption' in its everyday meaning instead of formal approval

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'How does a government make a public policy? Does someone just wake up and announce it?'
teach.praise: Wow! First spot the problem, ask the people affected, draft options, get approval, put it into action and keep improving it. That's a proper policy cycle!
teach.nudge: What comes after spotting the problem? Who should be asked, and what happens once the policy is approved?

topics.title: Putting policies into action and checking results

learn.hook: A village planted 1,000 saplings and celebrated. A year later, most had dried up. Was the policy a success? It depends on what you count!
points: Implementation means putting an approved policy into action. It is mainly done by the executive: ministries, departments, civil servants, district administrations and local bodies such as panchayats and municipalities. It needs money in the budget, trained people, clear rules and good coordination.
Many policies need several agencies to work together. For road safety near a school, the school, traffic police, road authorities and parents all have a part to play.
Monitoring means tracking progress while a policy is being carried out. Evaluation means judging, after some time, whether the policy achieved its goals and what its impact was.

An output is what was done (saplings planted, toilets built). An outcome is the real change (saplings surviving, toilets being used, fewer illnesses). Good evaluation checks outcomes and how different groups, such as girls, rural families or persons with disabilities, benefited.

Feedback and complaints show where a policy is falling short, so it can be revised. In a social audit, the community checks the records of a scheme in a public meeting. E-governance uses digital technology to deliver services, such as DigiLocker for documents, IRCTC for train tickets and the Parivahan portal for vehicle services, but people without internet access or digital skills still need offline help.

example.q: Think it through: A ward planted 1,000 saplings. After one year, only 350 were alive. What went wrong, and how can it be fixed?
steps: The output looked good: 1,000 saplings planted.
The outcome was weak: 1,000 - 350 = 650 saplings died.
Likely causes: no plan for watering, no tree guards, and no one responsible for checking survival.
Fix: give one agency clear responsibility, budget for watering and guards, involve residents, and monitor survival every few months.
example.answer: Implementation and monitoring were weak. Counting plantings is not enough; survival (the outcome) must be planned for and checked.

learn.reallife: Many services that once needed long queues can now be done online: you can book train tickets on IRCTC, and families can keep marksheets and other certificates in DigiLocker. Common Service Centres help people who cannot do this on their own.

games.title: Action and results: true or false?
items: A good policy on paper can still fail if it is poorly implemented.
Without money, trained staff and coordination, even a well-designed policy may not reach people.
Monitoring is done only after a policy has completely ended.
Monitoring tracks progress while the policy is being carried out; evaluation judges the results later.
The number of saplings planted tells us how many saplings survived.
Planting is an output. Survival is the outcome, and it must be checked separately.
E-governance means using digital technology to deliver government services and information.
Examples include DigiLocker, online train ticket booking and online vehicle services.
Complaints from citizens can help a department find and fix gaps in a service.
Complaints are feedback that shows where a service is failing.
In a social audit, the community checks the records of a government scheme.
Social audits let local people verify whether money was spent and work was done as recorded.

items.text: Putting an approved policy into action is called ___.
The number of toilets built is an ___; families actually using them is an outcome.
Judging the results and impact of a policy after some time is called ___.
DigiLocker lets people store and share ___ copies of their documents.

quiz.q: Who mainly implements public policies?
options: Ministries, departments, civil servants and local bodies
quiz.explain: Implementation is the work of the executive: ministries, departments, civil servants, district offices, panchayats and municipalities.
quiz.mistake: Thinks courts or the media carry out policies

quiz.q: What is the difference between monitoring and evaluation?
options: Monitoring tracks progress while a policy runs; evaluation judges its results and impact later
Monitoring happens before a policy is made; evaluation happens on election day
They mean exactly the same thing
Evaluation is done only by foreign countries
quiz.explain: Monitoring is ongoing tracking during implementation. Evaluation looks back to judge whether goals were achieved.
quiz.mistake: Treats monitoring and evaluation as the same step

quiz.q: A ward installed 40 public water taps. A survey found that 30 of them were working. How many taps were NOT working?
quiz.explain: Taps not working = 40 - 30 = 10. Finding such gaps is exactly what monitoring is for.
quiz.mistake: Adds the numbers or picks a number given in the question
steps: Total taps = 40
Working taps = 30
Not working = 40 - 30 = 10

quiz.q: Which of these is an OUTCOME rather than an output of a clean-water policy?
options: Fewer children falling ill with diarrhoea
quiz.explain: An outcome is a real change in people's lives, such as better health. Pipelines, money and meetings are inputs or outputs.
quiz.mistake: Confuses activity done (output) with real change (outcome)

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of e-governance?
options: Getting a vehicle-related service on the Parivahan portal
Buying vegetables at a weekly market
Playing an online game with friends
Sending a birthday greeting by post
quiz.explain: E-governance is the use of digital technology to deliver government services. The Parivahan portal offers vehicle-related services online.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any online activity is e-governance

quiz.q: A certificate service is made online-only. What problem might this create?
options: Nobody will ever need the certificate
People without internet access or digital skills may be left out, so offline help is also needed
quiz.explain: Not everyone has a smartphone, internet or digital skills. Inclusive governance keeps help centres or offline options for them.
quiz.mistake: Assumes everyone can use online services equally

quiz.q: What happens in a social audit?
options: A private company checks its own profits
Local people check the records of a government scheme in a public meeting
quiz.explain: In a social audit, the community examines records of a scheme, such as work done and money spent, to check that they match reality.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a social audit with a financial check inside a company

quiz.q: A tree-planting drive counted saplings planted but never checked how many survived. What was the main weakness?
options: Monitoring looked only at outputs, and no one was responsible for watering and protecting the saplings
The saplings were planted on a weekend
quiz.explain: Counting plantings measures only the output. Without care after planting and checks on survival, the real goal, a greener area, is not met.
quiz.mistake: Judges success by activity done instead of the result achieved

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'Once a policy is approved, the job is finished, right? Who carries it out, and how do we know if it worked?'
teach.praise: So the job is NOT finished! Departments carry it out, we monitor and evaluate the real outcomes, and feedback helps fix it. Super sapling-saving thinking!
teach.nudge: Who actually puts the policy into action? And how do we check whether it really changed things?

learn.hook: You don't need to be a minister to improve governance. Reporting one broken streetlight can make a whole lane safer!
points: Voting is important, but citizens' role does not end on election day. Between elections, people can give feedback, take part in public consultations, raise complaints and suggest ideas.

In villages, the Gram Sabha includes every adult whose name is on the voter list of the village or panchayat area. It discusses village plans and reviews the work done. The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (1992) gave constitutional status to panchayats and municipalities.

The Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005 lets any citizen ask a public authority for information. A reply is normally due within 30 days, or within 48 hours if a person's life or liberty is involved. This supports transparency and accountability.
Citizens can lodge complaints online through CPGRAMS (the Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System), use helplines, and share ideas on programmes through the MyGov platform.

Everyday duties also matter: following rules, paying taxes, saving water and electricity, safeguarding public property (a Fundamental Duty) and checking information before forwarding it. Students can join student councils, cleanliness drives and road-safety campaigns.

example.q: Think it through: The streetlight on your lane has not worked for two weeks. What can your family do?
steps: Note the exact location and the pole number, if there is one.
Report it to the municipal helpline, app or website, or tell the ward councillor.
Keep the complaint number and follow up if nothing happens.
If there is still no action, an RTI application can ask for the status of the complaint.
example.answer: Report it through the proper channel, keep a record, and follow up. Active citizens help governance work better.

learn.reallife: National Good Governance Day is observed on 25 December, the birth anniversary of former Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee. In the Swachh Survekshan cleanliness survey, citizens' feedback is part of how cities are ranked; Indore and Surat were jointly ranked the cleanest cities in Swachh Survekshan 2023.

games.title: Tools for active citizens
pairs: Ask a public authority for information
Villagers discuss and review village plans
Lodge a complaint online with government departments
Share ideas and suggestions on government programmes
Students take part in school decisions

items.q: Year the RTI Act was passed?
Normal days allowed for an RTI reply?
Hours allowed for an RTI reply if life or liberty is at stake?
Date of National Good Governance Day?
Village assembly of all adult voters?
Amendment that gave panchayats constitutional status?

quiz.q: Which of these is a way for citizens to take part in governance BETWEEN elections?
options: Attending a Gram Sabha meeting to discuss village plans
Waiting five years and doing nothing
Damaging public property to show anger
quiz.explain: Gram Sabha meetings let villagers discuss plans and review work. Participation continues between elections.
quiz.mistake: Thinks citizens can take part only by voting

quiz.q: Who are the members of a Gram Sabha?
options: Only the sarpanch and the panchayat secretary
All adults whose names are on the voter list of the village or panchayat area
Only government officers posted in the village
All children studying in the village school
quiz.explain: The Gram Sabha is made up of every adult registered as a voter in the village or panchayat area, so it is the village's own assembly.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the Gram Sabha with the elected panchayat

quiz.q: What does the Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005 allow?
options: Any citizen can ask public authorities for information
Only journalists can read government files
Citizens can make new laws on their own
quiz.explain: Under the RTI Act, any citizen can seek information from public authorities, which makes government more transparent and accountable.
quiz.mistake: Thinks RTI is only for journalists or gives law-making power

quiz.q: Under the RTI Act, within how much time should a normal request usually be answered?
quiz.explain: A reply is normally due within 30 days. If a person's life or liberty is involved, it must be given within 48 hours.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a shorter or longer time limit

quiz.q: National Good Governance Day is observed every year on:
quiz.explain: Good Governance Day is observed on 25 December, the birth anniversary of former Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee.
quiz.mistake: Mixes it up with other national days

quiz.q: Which is the most helpful thing a student can do to support good governance?
options: Forward every message to all groups immediately
Check whether information is true before sharing it
Throw waste on the road because cleaners will pick it up
quiz.explain: Checking information before forwarding stops rumours, which helps people and authorities make good decisions.
quiz.mistake: Does not see everyday behaviour as part of governance

quiz.q: Which of these is one of the Fundamental Duties of Indian citizens?
options: To live in a big city
quiz.explain: Safeguarding public property and avoiding violence is a Fundamental Duty listed in Article 51A of the Constitution.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up duties with personal choices

quiz.q: Why is feedback from citizens useful to the government?
options: It is not useful, because officials know everything
Citizens use services every day and notice problems that officials may miss
It replaces the need for any departments
It lets citizens avoid following rules
quiz.explain: People who use a service daily see its gaps first. Their feedback helps departments fix problems and improve policies.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only officials can spot problems in services

teach.ask: Gappu hops onto your book: 'I'm just a small bird. Can ordinary people like you and me really do anything for governance?'
teach.praise: Yay! We can vote, join the Gram Sabha, give feedback and complaints, ask questions using RTI, and do our duties every day. Even small birds count!
teach.nudge: Voting is one way. What else can citizens do between elections, and how can they ask the government for information?
